newsitem.title: CHINA: China inflation seen 2.0 pct this year-economist.
newsitem.headline: China inflation seen 2.0 pct this year-economist.

text.p: China's benchmark retail price inflation could be as low as 2.0 percent this year, well down from a government-set target of 6.0 percent, said Qiu Xiaohua, chief economist of the State Statistical Bureau.
He recommended the government focus on stabilising prices rather than simply cutting them, referring to China's policy launched about three years ago to curb inflation through administrative means.
The China Daily Business Weekly on Sunday quoted Qiu as saying he saw a retail price inflation rate of 6.0 percent as normal for China while the rate should be about 3.0-4.0 percent in the long-term.
China's January-July inflation was 1.6 percent -- its lowest level since the mid-1980s, he said.,

Retail price inflation slowed to 0.6 percent year-on-year in July, down from 0.8 percent in June and May, official figures showed. Consumer price inflation rose 2.7 percent in July alone and 3.9 percent for January-July.
Qiu attributed the fall -- from 6.1 percent last year compared with 14.8 percent in 1995 and a communist-era high of 21.7 percent the year before -- to several factors.
Record grain harvests in 1995 and 1996 coupled with a good summer harvest this year had effectively solved the imbalance between supply and demand of agricultural products, he said.
In 1994, 65 percent of inflation was caused by high food prices while in the first half of this year, food accounted for just one-sixth of inflation, he said.
Retail prices showed that food accounted for 48 percent of consumer spending.
Imports of grain and oil products had prevented imbalances in supply and demand, Qui said.
A tight monetary policy had helped to reduce overall demand, with investment showing little increase in the first half, thus holding prices of production materials, he said.
Qui did not refer to concerns voiced by some economists that demand has slumped this year, leading to deflationary concerns.
However, he said macro-economic controls had prevented expenditures from racing out of control, and the strength of the domestic yuan currency had eased earlier speculation on a major depreciation.
"We should take this rare opportunity to speed up the reform of state-owned firms, the housing system, as well as investment and price structures," Qiu was quoted as saying.
Accelerated housing reform would help the state to recoup nearly 100 billion yuan ($12 billion) in capital tied up in 50 million square metres of unsold housing nationwide, he said.
At present, most of China's estimated 200 million urban residents are allocated cheap or virtually free housing from their employers, hampering efforts to create a real housing market.

Low inflation makes it easier for China's lumbering state enterprises to lift the brakes from paring surplus labour, he said, referring to a reform that has been held back for years amid fears of social unrest.
Low inflation also forces manufacturers to cut prices to survive fierce competition, thus pushing them to move away from production of unsellable goods, Qiu said.
